title: ジャズと自由と秩序  (Jazz, Freedom, and Order)

segments.t: Poseidon president Ikezawa brings Muranishi and Toshi to an upscale jazz lounge run by Reika. As live music fills the room, Muranishi admires how freely the band plays, and Ikezawa replies with a pointed lesson about unspoken rules and order. Listen first to the contrast between Reika's velvet club hospitality and Ikezawa's gravelly boss talk.
よう、ママ、久しぶり。
いらっしゃいませ。
こちらでございます、どうぞ。
まあ、飲んで。
麗華です。どうぞごひいきに。
この店、任せたんだ。
気に入ったかな？
皆さん、自由に演奏してて楽しそうです。
ジャズのセッションってのは自由にやってるように見える。
でもな、暗黙の決まり事があるんだよ。
そうなんですね。
自由と秩序のバランスがいいからなんだ。
池沢さん、そろそろ要件を聞きたいですね。
From lounge greetings to a veiled warning disguised as music talk, every speaker picks a distinct level of polish. Let's hear the highlights.
よう、ママ、久しぶり。

'Hey, Mama-san, long time no see.' In Japan, a woman who runs a lounge or bar is affectionately called "mama". "Hisashiburi" is the warm, everyday greeting for 'it has been a while'—add "desu" when speaking politely.
いらっしゃいませ。
'Welcome.' Walk into any shop, restaurant, or lounge in Japan and staff will greet you with "irasshaimase", a welcoming expression built on an honorific root for coming in.
こちらでございます、どうぞ。
'Right this way, please.' "Kochira" is the polite cousin of "koko", here or this way, and "de gozaimasu" elevates plain "desu" to five-star hospitality before "douzo", please go ahead.
まあ、飲んで。
'Come on, have a drink.' "Nonde" comes from "nomu", to drink, and on its own without "kudasai" it lands like a relaxed host urging guests to drink up.
どうぞごひいきに。
'Thank you for your patronage.' Classic merchant poise: "hiiki" means special favor or support, and "go-hiiki ni" politely asks a guest to become a regular.
気に入ったかな？
'Do you like it here?' Idiomatic "ki ni itta" literally says something 'entered your spirit' ("ki"), which is how Japanese expresses taking a liking to a place or song.
皆さん、自由に演奏してて楽しそうです。

'Everyone is playing freely and looks like they are having fun.' "Jiyuu ni" turns "jiyuu", freedom, into 'freely'. At the end, dropping the final sound of "tanoshii", fun, and adding "sou desu" means 'looks fun'.
でもな、暗黙の決まり事があるんだよ。
'Still, there are unspoken rules.' "Anmoku" means silent or unspoken, linked by "no" to "kimarigoto", settled rules or understandings, before "aru n da yo" drives the warning home.
そうなんですね。
'Is that so?' Built on "sou", that way, "sou nan desu ne" receives new information smoothly—closer to 'ah, I see how that is' than a full agreement.
自由と秩序のバランスがいいからなんだ。

'It is because the balance between freedom and order is so good.' "Jiyuu to chitsujo" pairs "jiyuu", freedom, with "chitsujo", social order, using "to" for 'and', then wraps the reason in "ii kara nan da", 'it is because it is good'.
池沢さん、そろそろ要件を聞きたいですね。

'Mr. Ikezawa, I would like to hear your main point soon.' "Sorosoro" hints gently that it is about time to move on. "Youken" means the real business at hand, and "kikitai" attaches "tai", want to, onto "kiku", hear. Now let's listen to the whole lounge conversation again from start to finish.
よう、ママ、久しぶり。
いらっしゃいませ。
こちらでございます、どうぞ。
まあ、飲んで。
麗華です。どうぞごひいきに。
この店、任せたんだ。
気に入ったかな？
皆さん、自由に演奏してて楽しそうです。
ジャズのセッションってのは自由にやってるように見える。
でもな、暗黙の決まり事があるんだよ。
そうなんですね。
自由と秩序のバランスがいいからなんだ。
池沢さん、そろそろ要件を聞きたいですね。
Keep "hisashiburi" handy for reunions, "ki ni itta" for saying you like a place, and "sorosoro" whenever it is time to wrap up or get to the point. Until next scene, see you again.
また会いましょう。
